Selected F-NUSPEC-CODEPAGES-GAP as the most consequential CONTRADICTED fact (a claimed real-world runtime packaging defect, vs. F-APITYPE-COUNT-SELFCONSISTENCY's cosmetic doc count mismatch which was already independently reproduced in C3). Reproduced from scratch: scaffolded a brand-new net8.0 console app, ran `dotnet add package Aspose.Words.FOSS` exactly as the README's Getting Started section instructs, inspected obj/project.assets.json -- confirmed the restored dependency graph for net8.0 contains only Aspose.Words.FOSS, BitMiracle.LibTiff.NET, SkiaSharp(+native assets); zero reference to System.Text.Encoding.CodePages, exactly as facts.json claims. Also restored a separate net6.0 console app (forcing NuGet to resolve the package's netstandard2.0 asset group instead of its net8.0 group) and confirmed the same gap there (System.Text.Encoding.CodePages absent from that graph too). This much of facts.json's claim is independently CONFIRMED. Root cause found: System.Text.Encoding.CodePages.dll ships as part of the installed Microsoft.NETCore.App shared framework itself (confirmed present at C:\Program Files\dotnet\shared\Microsoft.NETCore.App\8.0.21\System.Text.Encoding.CodePages.dll and the 10.0.x folders) -- this is standard, well-documented .NET Core 3.0+/.NET 5+ behavior: the type resolves from the shared framework's trusted-platform-assembly list at runtime even when the app's own bin output (confirmed: bin/Debug/net8.0/ contains no System.Text.Encoding.CodePages.dll) and project.assets.json never reference the package. The claimed consequence does not reproduce under the only consumption scenario the README itself documents (a default, framework-dependent `dotnet add package` + run).

findings.title: The candidate never once uses the mandated 'Enterprise Edition' naming -- zero compliant occurrences in the entire document
findings.detail: Added by a second independent pass of this same review session. MISSION_AUTHORITY.md requires the aspose.com commercial product be named 'Enterprise Edition' everywhere, with no substitute wording ('commercial', 'paid version', etc.). `grep -ni 'enterprise edition'` against lane_l_candidate.md returns zero matches. Instead the document repeatedly uses 'commercial' as a substitute name at visitor-facing identity positions: line 85 ('get it right away in the commercial [Aspose.Words for .NET]'), line 95 ('the same as the commercial product'), line 150 ('the same as in the commercial Aspose.Words for .NET'), line 915 ('the commercial [Aspose.Words for .NET] has all of it'), line 944 ('matches the commercial [Aspose.Words for .NET]'). (Lines 907/913/932/961 use 'commercial' in a different, non-naming sense -- 'commercial offering'/'commercial codebase'/'commercial source'/MIT's standard 'commercial and personal use' -- and are not counted as violations.) This is a total gap, not a partial one: unlike the sibling aspose-words-foss/Aspose.Words-FOSS-for-Python candidate reviewed in the same session (which has 1 compliant usage alongside 3 non-compliant ones) and aspose-slides-foss/Aspose.Slides-FOSS-for-Java (1 compliant usage alongside 2 non-compliant ones), this document contains no instance of the correct phrasing anywhere to model the fix on. Neither facts.json, content_units.json, nor lane_r_plan.md registers naming-standard compliance as a checked dimension.
findings.recommendation: Replace each 'commercial [Aspose.Words for .NET]' / 'the commercial product' / 'the commercial Aspose.Words for .NET' identity reference with 'Aspose.Words for .NET — Enterprise Edition' (full name, per MISSION_AUTHORITY's required phrasing) at first use per section, with an unambiguous pronoun or short back-reference permissible afterward within the same paragraph.

findings.title: F-NUSPEC-CODEPAGES-GAP's claimed runtime-failure consequence does not reproduce under the README's own documented consumption scenario
findings.detail: facts.json's F-NUSPEC-CODEPAGES-GAP and draft_upstream_issue.md's 'Impact' section both claim a consumer who does exactly what the README's Getting Started section instructs ('dotnet add package Aspose.Words.FOSS' and nothing else) 'risks a runtime load failure' / 'risks a runtime assembly load failure' the first time the Document class's static constructor runs, because the published nuspec omits System.Text.Encoding.CodePages as a dependency for the netstandard2.0 and net8.0 asset groups. I independently reproduced the omission itself (confirmed: true, for both a net8.0 and a net6.0 consumer's restored dependency graph) but then went one step further and actually ran the exact scenario described -- a fresh net8.0 console app, `dotnet add package Aspose.Words.FOSS`, then `new Document();` as the only statement. It ran to completion with no exception. The reason: System.Text.Encoding.CodePages.dll ships as part of the installed Microsoft.NETCore.App shared framework for every currently-supported .NET Core 3.0+/.NET 5+ target (confirmed present on disk in both the 8.0.21 and 10.0.x shared-framework folders), so the CLR resolves the type from there at runtime regardless of whether the consuming app's own bin output or NuGet-restored graph references the package -- which is exactly what was observed (bin/Debug/net8.0/ has no System.Text.Encoding.CodePages.dll, yet the type loaded and ran successfully). The nuspec gap is real as a metadata-hygiene defect, but the severity/impact framing used to justify filing a new upstream issue is not supported by actual execution evidence, and the task's own instruction treats an un-reproducible claim from the most consequential CONTRADICTED fact as reject-worthy.
findings.recommendation: Before this issue is filed upstream, correct facts.json's severity note and draft_upstream_issue.md's 'Impact' section: drop or heavily qualify the 'runtime load failure' framing (directly refuted for the default framework-dependent scenario the README documents), and reframe this as a nuspec/package-metadata hygiene gap -- real but latent for ordinary consumers -- unless and until a genuinely failing scenario (e.g. a trimmed self-contained publish, which was not tested by either this review or the original facts.json) is itself independently reproduced and cited as the actual risk.

verdict_rationale: Both REJECT grounds were fixed by the supervisor session 2026-10-21, after independently re-verifying each before acting on it. F2 (total Enterprise Edition naming gap): all 5 non-compliant 'commercial'-as-name occurrences (lines 85, 95, 150, 915, 944 of the live README) were corrected to 'Aspose.Words for .NET — Enterprise Edition' in lane_l_candidate.md; the 4 occurrences the finding itself identified as non-naming uses ('commercial offering', 'commercial codebase', 'commercial source', MIT's 'commercial and personal use') were left untouched. The pre-existing 615/617 count fix was left exactly as is, per instruction. A fresh `diff -u` against a newly re-fetched live README (source_revision/readme_blob_sha both reconfirmed unchanged -- no drift) shows exactly these 6 hunks (1 count fix + 5 naming fixes) and nothing else; lane_l_candidate.diff has been extended to cover all 6. F1 (F-NUSPEC-CODEPAGES-GAP's overstated severity): independently re-reproduced the review's own finding before trusting it -- ran the README's exact Quick Start (`dotnet add package Aspose.Words.FOSS` into a fresh net8.0 console app, then `new Document()`) and it completed with no exception, confirming C6's result. Went further than the review did: also tested a self-contained publish and a trimmed self-contained publish of the same app, and `System.Text.Encoding.CodePages.dll` was present and loaded successfully in both, because the .NET SDK's implicit `Microsoft.NETCore.App` framework reference supplies that assembly for any net5.0+/netstandard2.0-via-net8.0 project regardless of what the package's own nuspec declares. facts.json's F-NUSPEC-CODEPAGES-GAP has been corrected: the nuspec dependency-declaration gap itself remains a real, independently-reconfirmed metadata defect (still CONTRADICTED), but its severity/evidence text no longer claims a reproduced 'runtime load failure' -- it now states plainly that this consequence did not reproduce under framework-dependent, self-contained, or trimmed self-contained consumption, and that only a narrower, untested, non-SDK-style scenario remains unverified. draft_upstream_issue.md's title and Impact section were corrected to match: the draft is now explicit that this is a packaging-metadata hygiene gap, not a demonstrated runtime failure, before any filing decision is made. Verdict updated from REJECT to ACCEPT after both fixes; this is not a retroactive downgrade of either finding -- F1 and F2 stand as correctly identified and are marked 'fixed', not erased, per this project's AGENTS.md re-reporting discipline. Everything the original review found sound (the 615/617 fix itself, content_units.json's section-by-section completeness, the upstream dedup check, Lane R's convergence reasoning) is unchanged and still holds.
